screens.title: Peer and Chaincode Deployment on Kubernetes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll join the piece of the Fabric puzzle that runs the ledger and executes chaincode: the Peer. We start from the assumptions that your Certificate Authorities and Orderers are already running in Kubernetes, and then focus on how to deploy peers reliably with StatefulSets so they keep stable identities and persistent storage. You will learn why peers need Persistent Volume Claims for /var/hyperledger/production, how CouchDB can run as its own stateful service, and how cryptographic material is securely mounted into peer pods with Secrets and ConfigMaps. We also cover how to perform one-off administrative tasks — creating channels, joining peers, and running chaincode lifecycle commands — using Kubernetes Job resources that run fabric-tools containers to completion. Finally, you will see the practical flow for packaging, installing, approving, and committing chaincode on a Fabric channel and common pitfalls to avoid, such as missing PVC bindings or incorrect service endpoints. By the end you will understand the manifests, the runtime concerns, and the verification steps you need to keep peers healthy and chaincode deployable.

screens.title: Why Peers are Stateful and why StatefulSets
screens.narratorSegment: Peers are the structural core of a Fabric network: they host the ledger, maintain world state, and run chaincode that endorses transactions. Because a peer stores mutable ledger data on disk under /var/hyperledger/production, it cannot be treated as an ephemeral pod. If a pod restarts or gets rescheduled, losing that directory means losing the ledger state. Kubernetes StatefulSets provide stable network identities and let you define volumeClaimTemplates so each replica gets its own persistent volume claim. This preserves ledger continuity across restarts. In practice, a peer StatefulSet specifies the hyperledger/fabric-peer image, mounts for MSP and TLS, and environment variables such as CORE_PEER_ID, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED, and CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE. A common misconception is to treat peers like stateless microservices; doing so causes data loss. A quick concrete example: if peer0 restarts and its PVC was not bound, the peer will start with an empty ledger and will fail to sync until you restore or reseed the ledger. Key verification steps include confirming each pod has a bound PVC and that the peer sees its MSP and TLS files mounted correctly. A final takeaway: treat peers as stateful first-class citizens and plan storage and identity mounts when you design manifests.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Why Peers are Stateful
Definition

A peer stores ledger and chaincode artifacts on disk and must retain those files across restarts. Treat peers as stateful workloads and use StatefulSets to give each replica a stable DNS name and persistent storage.

Essential env vars
CORE_PEER_ID, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED, CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE
Common misconception
Treating peers as ephemeral causes ledger loss; ensure PVCs are configured and bound for production readiness.
Manifest snippet (conceptual)
# StatefulSet excerpt
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: peer0-org1
spec:
  serviceName: peer0-org1
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: peer0
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: peer
        image: hyperledger/fabric-peer:latest
        env:
        - name: CORE_PEER_ID
          value: peer0.org1.example.com
        - name: CORE_PEER_ADDRESS
          value: peer0-org1.org1.svc.cluster.local:7051
        volumeMounts:
        - name: ledger-data
          mountPath: /var/hyperledger/production
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: ledger-data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: standard
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
Key Takeaway

StatefulSets plus volumeClaimTemplates ensure each peer replica has a stable identity and durable disk for the ledger.

screens.title: Peer Manifest Components and Environment Variables
screens.narratorSegment: A peer StatefulSet is more than an image reference; it codifies the peer's runtime identity, storage, and security posture. The main components to include are the container image (hyperledger/fabric-peer), the environment variables that tell the peer its identity and TLS configuration, mounts for MSP and TLS secrets, and a volumeClaimTemplates block for ledger persistence. Environment variables like CORE_PEER_ID and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS establish how the peer identifies itself on the network. CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID sets the organization MSP ID, and CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED controls whether TLS is required. If you use CouchDB, CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE should be set to couchdb and the address provided via CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS. A common error is referencing service names that don't exist; double-check service DNS names and ports, and confirm that the CouchDB service is reachable from the peer namespace. As a practical check, ensure your CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH and TLS cert paths point to mounted secrets. When you roll out the StatefulSet, verify pod startup, PVC binding, and that the peer logs show a successful identity load. These pieces together make a robust peer manifest for production Kubernetes deployments. Peer Manifest Components and Environment Variables means include image, env vars for identity and tls, mounts for secrets, and pvc templates; verify service names and bound pvcs at rollout.. In practical terms, what to include in your statefulset and why each item matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Manifest Components
Primary fields to define
  • Image and resources: use a specific fabric-peer image and resource limits appropriate for endorsement load.
  • Environment variables: CORE_PEER_ID, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED, and CouchDB address if used.
  • Secrets & ConfigMaps: mount MSP and TLS artifacts as volumes and point CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH accordingly.
  • volumeClaimTemplates: ensure persistent storage is requested for ledger data.
Quick check
After apply, run kubectl get pods and kubectl describe pvc to confirm each peer pod has a bound PVC and the expected mounted volumes.
Environment variables example
env:
- name: CORE_PEER_ID
  value: peer0.org1.example.com
- name: CORE_PEER_ADDRESS
  value: peer0-org1.org1.svc.cluster.local:7051
- name: CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID
  value: Org1MSP
- name: CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED
  value: "true"
- name: CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE
  value: couchdb
- name: CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS
  value: couchdb-org1-0.couchdb-org1:5984
Common mistake

Using the wrong service DNS for CouchDB or Orderer will block peer connectivity. Always test DNS resolution from the peer pod if startup fails.

screens.title: Persistent Storage and CouchDB Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Persistent storage is essential to maintain peer ledger integrity. For the peer's /var/hyperledger/production directory, define a PersistentVolumeClaim through the StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates so each peer replica receives its own PVC. If your cluster supports dynamic provisioning, reference a StorageClass; otherwise pre-provision PVs matching the access mode and capacity. When using CouchDB as the state database, deploy CouchDB as its own StatefulSet and expose it with a headless Service so peers can reach particular CouchDB instances. The peer should reference that service through CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS. A practical scenario: create couchdb-org1-statefulset. yaml and couchdb-org1-service. yaml with a PVC template for each CouchDB pod. After applying both StatefulSets, ensure the CouchDB pods report Running and their PVCs are Bound. Common pitfalls include PVCs left unbound due to an incorrect storage class or insufficient capacity, which will prevent peers from starting and cause ledger loss. Always verify PV/PVC status and pod events if a peer pod remains pending. The key is to design storage with replication and retention suitable for your availability needs and confirm mounts at runtime. Persistent Storage and CouchDB Integration means ensure pvcs bind and couchdb is deployed with its own pvcs; check storageclass settings and pod events when issues arise.. In practical terms, pvcs for ledger data and a separate statefulset for couchdb when using document store. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Persistent Storage
VolumeClaimTemplate pattern

Use the StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates to request durable storage per replica. Choose access mode ReadWriteOnce for single-writer ledger directories and size according to expected ledger growth.

volumeClaimTemplates:
- metadata:
    name: ledger-data
  spec:
    accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
    storageClassName: standard
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 20Gi
CouchDB service example
# Peer env var to point to CouchDB
- name: CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS
  value: couchdb-org1-0.couchdb-org1:5984
Troubleshooting tip

If the peer cannot reach CouchDB, exec into the peer pod and test DNS resolution and connection to the couchdb service name and port.

Check PV/PVC
kubectl get pvc and kubectl describe pv to ensure binding.
Pod events
Use kubectl describe pod to see events about mount failures or permission issues.
StorageClass
Confirm dynamic provisioning via a StorageClass when creating PVCs in production clusters.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Jobs for Admin Tasks
Job purpose and benefits
  • Run one-off fabric CLI commands reliably inside Kubernetes.
  • Mount crypto and channel artifacts so jobs are self-contained.
  • Track execution via kubectl get jobs and pod logs for auditing.
When to use
Channel create, peer join, install/approve/commit chaincode lifecycle steps—each fits a Job pattern.
Job YAML excerpt
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: join-peer0-org1-to-mychannel
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
      containers:
      - name: fabric-cli
        image: hyperledger/fabric-tools:latest
        env: [...CORE_PEER_ env vars...]
        command: ["/bin/bash","-c"]
        args:
          - |
            peer channel join -b /etc/hyperledger/fabric/channel-artifacts/mychannel.block
        volumeMounts:
        - name: channel-artifacts-volume
          mountPath: /etc/hyperledger/fabric/channel-artifacts
      volumes:
      - name: channel-artifacts-volume
        configMap:
          name: channel-artifacts-cm
Debugging
kubectl logs and kubectl describe pod to view errors or missing mounts.
Idempotency
Design Jobs to be safe to re-run or to fail clearly so operators can retry deterministically.
Audit
Jobs provide a Kubernetes-native audit trail of administrative commands and their results.

screens.title: Channel Creation and Peer Join Job Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete join Job example to make the process concrete. The Job runs a fabric-tools container that has the peer CLI available and mounts three main things: the peer MSP/TLS secrets, the orderer TLS secret, and channel-artifacts that contain mychannel. block. The Job sets CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED, CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, and ORDERER_TLS_ROOTCERT so the peer CLI can authenticate and reach both peer and orderer endpoints. The command executed is peer channel join -b. After applying the join-job. yaml, monitor the Job with kubectl get jobs, find the job pod using the job-name label, and inspect logs with kubectl logs to confirm the join succeeded. A common contrast here: using a Deployment for the same command would leave a long-running pod; a Job ensures the pod terminates on completion, which is the right semantics for one-off admin tasks. If the job pod fails, check volume mounts, file permissions, and environment values for typos. This step is crucial because a successful join is a prerequisite before committing chaincode definitions to a channel. In practical terms, a concrete job yaml to join a peer to an existing channel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: A Job runs fabric-tools, mounts crypto and channel artifacts, executes peer channel join, and terminates for clear auditability.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Channel Join Job
Narrated Job steps
  1. Prepare mychannel.block in a ConfigMap named channel-artifacts-cm.
  2. Create a Job that mounts MSP and TLS secrets and the channel artifact.
  3. Run peer channel join -b /etc/hyperledger/fabric/channel-artifacts/mychannel.block.
  4. Verify success via kubectl logs and kubectl get jobs.
Why Jobs?
Jobs provide a clean lifecycle for admin commands and surface success/failure within the cluster.
Join Job (excerpt)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: join-peer0-org1-to-mychannel
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
      containers:
      - name: fabric-cli
        image: hyperledger/fabric-tools:latest
        env:
        - name: CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED
          value: "true"
        - name: CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID
          value: Org1MSP
        - name: CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH
          value: /etc/hyperledger/fabric/msp
        - name: CORE_PEER_ADDRESS
          value: peer0-org1.org1.example.com:7051
        command: ["/bin/bash","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          peer channel join -b /etc/hyperledger/fabric/channel-artifacts/mychannel.block
        volumeMounts:
        - name: channel-artifacts-volume
          mountPath: /etc/hyperledger/fabric/channel-artifacts
      volumes:
      - name: channel-artifacts-volume
        configMap:
          name: channel-artifacts-cm

screens.title: Chaincode Lifecycle Using Kubernetes Jobs
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying chaincode on a Kubernetes-managed Fabric network follows the standard Fabric lifecycle but each step can be executed inside Jobs so the cluster tracks work and artifacts. The lifecycle steps are: package the chaincode into a tar. gz with peer lifecycle chaincode package, install the package on each peer using peer lifecycle chaincode install, have each organization approve the chaincode definition using peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg, and finally commit the chaincode definition with peer lifecycle chaincode commit once enough approvals exist. In Kubernetes, create a sequence of Jobs for each step or a single Job that runs a script performing the ordered steps. Chaincode source can be baked into the fabric-tools image for development, or mounted from a ConfigMap or shared Persistent Volume in more advanced scenarios. Use explicit package IDs from the install output and forward them to approval commands. A misconception is assuming chaincode install auto-approves the definition; install is local to a peer, but approval is an org-level configuration step recorded on the channel. Always capture Job logs and check approval status with peer lifecycle chaincode queryapproved to confirm readiness before committing. Organizing lifecycle steps as Jobs makes chaincode operations reproducible and CI-friendly.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Chaincode Lifecycle
Lifecycle steps
  1. Package chaincode with peer lifecycle chaincode package to create a tar.gz.
  2. Install package on peers with peer lifecycle chaincode install and capture package ID.
  3. Approve definition for each org using peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg.
  4. Commit the chaincode definition once approval thresholds are met using peer lifecycle chaincode commit.
Packaging options
Include chaincode in the fabric-tools image for dev, or mount from ConfigMap/PV for CI/CD and production workflows.
Install & approve (snippet)
# Example commands run inside a Job container
peer lifecycle chaincode package mycc.tar.gz --path ./chaincode --lang golang --label mycc_1
peer lifecycle chaincode install mycc.tar.gz
# capture package id from install output and use in approve
peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg --package-id  --sequence 1 --channelID mychannel
peer lifecycle chaincode commit --channelID mychannel --name mycc --sequence 1

screens.title: Chaincode Packaging Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: When you prepare chaincode for deployment in Kubernetes, you have three common strategies: bake chaincode into a custom fabric-tools image, mount the chaincode from a ConfigMap, or provide it via a shared Persistent Volume. Baking chaincode into an image simplifies development and ensures the package is available when the Job runs, but it requires image builds and pushes for each chaincode change. Using ConfigMaps works for small codebases and quick iteration, but ConfigMaps have size limitations and are less suitable for large binary artifacts. A shared Persistent Volume allows larger artifacts and is convenient in CI/CD pipelines where build artifacts are stored centrally, but it requires PV lifecycle management and access controls. The chapter warns that for production you may prefer CI/CD-managed images or PVs to avoid ephemeral ConfigMap limitations. A common misconception is that installing chaincode on a peer equals committing it to the channel — install is local, while approval and commit are channel operations that must be coordinated. Choose the packaging approach that fits your workflow: image for controlled release, PV for large teams and CI, and ConfigMap for small demos and quick tests.

keyIdea.text: Use images for reproducible releases, PV for larger CI/CD pipelines, and ConfigMaps only for small or demo scenarios.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Packaging Comparison
Image-built chaincode
Pros: Reproducible, versioned, ideal for production. Cons: Image build overhead for each change.
ConfigMap-mounted source
Pros: Fast for demos and small code. Cons: Size limits and not ideal for binary artifacts.
Shared Persistent Volume
Pros: Works well with CI pipelines and large artifacts. Cons: Requires PV management and access control planning.
Key Takeaway

Pick a packaging approach that fits your release and CI processes; avoid ConfigMaps for large production chaincode artifacts.

screens.title: Secrets, ConfigMaps and mounting crypto material
screens.narratorSegment: Cryptographic materials must be provided to peers and to the fabric-tools containers that run admin commands. The recommended pattern is to generate MSP and TLS artifacts using fabric-ca-client or your chosen tooling, then place those artifacts into Kubernetes Secrets (for private keys and certs) and ConfigMaps (for non-sensitive artifacts like channel blocks). The peer StatefulSet mounts those Secrets at paths referenced by CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH and TLS variables so the peer loads its identity on startup. Jobs also mount the same secrets so fabric-tools can act as an org admin for channel creation and chaincode approval. A common mistake is encoding files incorrectly or placing private keys in non-secret ConfigMaps; always base64-encode and store sensitive files in Secrets. Another practical check is verifying file paths inside the running pod with kubectl exec to ensure the peer or job container sees the expected files and permissions. Remember that secrets mounted as files still respect Kubernetes RBAC and pod security policies, so align cluster-level security with your certificate handling practices. Proper secret management prevents startup failures and protects private keys in production environments. Secrets, ConfigMaps and mounting crypto material means store private keys in secrets, non-sensitive artifacts in configmaps, and verify mounted paths with kubectl exec after deployment.. In practical terms, how to inject msps, tls certs, and channel artifacts securely into pods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Secrets & ConfigMaps
Where to store what
  • Private keys and TLS certs: Kubernetes Secrets (base64-encoded).
  • Channel block artifacts and non-sensitive config: ConfigMaps or mounted PVs.
  • MSP directories should be mounted read-only into peer pods and job containers.
Verify mounts
After apply, exec into the pod and list the MSP and tls directories to confirm files exist and have expected permissions. Example: kubectl exec -it -- ls -la /etc/hyperledger/fabric/msp
Misconception

Storing private keys in ConfigMaps or as plain text is insecure and will complicate RBAC and audits.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Remediations
screens.narratorSegment: In production deployments, a few recurring problems tend to cause the most downtime. Incorrect service endpoints are common: if a peer's CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, ORDERER_ADDRESS, or CouchDB service names and ports are wrong, the peer or fabric CLI will fail to connect. Missing crypto material mounted incorrectly causes peers to fail at startup because MSP directories or TLS certs are not found. Persistent Volume issues—PVCs not binding to PVs—lead to peers starting with empty ledgers or failing to start entirely. Job failures often stem from incorrect peer CLI commands or missing environment variables and mounted files. Effective troubleshooting follows a pattern: check pod status and events with kubectl describe pod, inspect PVC and PV bindings with kubectl get pvc and kubectl describe pv, and view job pod logs with kubectl logs. For example, if a peer restarts and its ledger is empty, the most likely cause is an unbound PVC. If a job pod shows file-not-found errors, review volume mounts and ConfigMap/Secret names. These checks allow you to remediate quickly by fixing service names, recreating secrets, or provisioning PVs. Logging and consistent Jobs make it easier to reproduce and correct failures.

keyIdea.text: Use kubectl describe, get pvc, and job logs to find the root cause: endpoints, crypto mounts, PVC binding, or CLI errors.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Common Pitfalls
Incorrect service endpoints
Symptoms: connection refused, TLS handshake failures. Fix: verify service names and ports in env vars and test DNS from pods.
Missing crypto material
Symptoms: peer fails to start with MSP load errors. Fix: confirm Secrets exist, mounted paths match CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH and TLS paths.
PVC binding issues
Symptoms: pods Pending, empty ledger after restart. Fix: inspect storage class, ensure PVs are available or StorageClass supports dynamic provisioning.
Diagnostic checklist
  • kubectl describe pod
  • kubectl get pvc
  • kubectl logs
Remediation tips
Correct service names, recreate or rebind secrets, provision PVs, and fix job commands. Repeat and verify with logs.

screens.title: Activity: Deploy Peer0.Org1 and Join Channel
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through the end-to-end steps to deploy peer0. org1, attach CouchDB, and join the peer to mychannel using a Job. Start by generating the peer's crypto with fabric-ca-client against your running CA: enroll the CA admin, register the peer identity, and enroll the peer to produce its MSP and TLS artifacts. Next, base64-encode required files and create Kubernetes Secrets for the peer MSP and TLS, plus a ConfigMap for the channel block artifact. Deploy CouchDB with a StatefulSet and Service ensuring a PVC template so the database persists. Then create a peer StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates for /var/hyperledger/production and mount the MSP and TLS secrets at the expected paths. Finally, create the join Job YAML which mounts the channel-artifacts ConfigMap and runs peer channel join -b /etc/hyperledger/fabric/channel-artifacts/mychannel. block. After applying each manifest, verify with kubectl get pods and kubectl get pvc. If the join Job fails, inspect the job pod logs and confirm that the mounted paths and environment variables match those in the peer StatefulSet. This activity reinforces manifest structure, secret management, and the Job execution pattern.

keyIdea.title: Lab workflow
keyIdea.text: Generate crypto, create Secrets/ConfigMaps, deploy CouchDB and peer StatefulSets with PVCs, then run a Job to join the peer to the channel.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Hands-on Activity
Step checklist
  1. Generate peer crypto with fabric-ca-client and copy MSP/TLS into a working directory.
  2. Create Secrets for peer MSP and TLS, and ConfigMap for mychannel.block.
  3. Deploy couchdb-org1 StatefulSet and service with PVC templates.
  4. Deploy peer0-org1 StatefulSet with PVCs and mounts for MSP/TLS.
  5. Create join Job to run peer channel join and monitor logs.
Command examples
# Example enroll and register commands
export FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_HOME=/tmp/peer0-org1
fabric-ca-client enroll -u https://peer0org1:peer0pw@:7054 --caname ca-org1 --tls.certfiles $FABRIC_CA_CLIENT_TLS_CERTFILES --mspdir ./crypto-config/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/msp

# Apply couchdb and peer manifests
kubectl apply -f couchdb-org1-statefulset.yaml -f couchdb-org1-service.yaml
kubectl apply -f peer0-org1-statefulset.yaml -f peer0-org1-service.yaml

# Create and monitor join job
kubectl apply -f join-peer-job.yaml
kubectl get jobs
kubectl get pods -l job-name=join-peer0-org1-to-mychannel
kubectl logs

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the essential ideas to carry forward. First, peer deployment must treat peers as stateful: use StatefulSets and PVCs to ensure stable identity and durable ledger storage. Third, the chaincode lifecycle remains packaging, installing, approving, and committing; each step can be run reliably inside Kubernetes Jobs so your operational steps are reproducible and auditable. Keep these three ideas in mind as you design manifests and run administrative operations in cluster environments. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll join the piece of the Fabric puzzle that runs the ledger and executes chaincode: the Peer. We start from the assumptions that your Certificate Authorities and Orderers are already running in Kubernetes, and then focus on how to deploy peers reliably with StatefulSets so they keep stable identities and persistent storage. You will learn why peers need Persistent Volume Claims for /var/hyperledger/production, how CouchDB can run as its own stateful service, and how cryptographic material is securely mounted into peer pods with Secrets and ConfigMaps. We also cover how to perform one-off administrative tasks — creating channels, joining peers, and running chaincode lifecycle commands — using Kubernetes Job resources that run fabric-tools containers to completion. Finally, you will see the practical flow for packaging, installing, approving, and committing chaincode on a Fabric channel and common pitfalls to avoid, such as missing PVC bindings or incorrect service endpoints. By the end you will understand the manifests, the runtime concerns, and the verification steps you need to keep peers healthy and chaincode deployable.

These learning objectives focus on the practical skills you need to deploy peers and chaincode on Kubernetes. First, you will design StatefulSet manifests for Peer nodes that provide stable network identities and persistent volume templates so ledger data survives restarts. Second, you will configure persistent storage using Persistent Volume Claims and connect a state database like CouchDB to a peer. Third, you'll learn to use Kubernetes Job resources to run fabric-cli operations, creating channels and joining peers programmatically inside K8s. Fourth, you'll form a working understanding of the chaincode lifecycle steps — packaging, installing, approving, and committing — and how Jobs can orchestrate those steps. Each objective emphasizes why the step matters in production and how it maps to typical manifest resources and runtime checks. Learning Objectives means design statefulsets, pvcs, and jobs to make peers durable and administrative tasks reproducible in kubernetes.. In practical terms, what you'll be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This second objectives screen goes deeper into operational tasks you will perform and verify. You will learn how to deploy CouchDB as a StatefulSet and connect it via the CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS environment variable so the peer uses CouchDB as its state database. You will configure Secrets and ConfigMaps to inject the peer's MSP and TLS materials, making sure CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH and TLS paths point to mounted volumes. You'll also learn to troubleshoot common issues such as PVC binding failures, incorrect service endpoints that block peer-to-orderer communication, and Job failures caused by missing environment variables or incorrect file mounts. Each objective stresses verification steps: kubectl get pods, kubectl logs, and checking job pod output. These operational skills reduce downtime and keep ledger integrity intact in production clusters. Learning Objectives — Operational Depth means integrate couchdb, mount crypto securely, and use logs and job status to troubleshoot peer and chaincode deployment issues.. Peers are the structural core of a Fabric network: they host the ledger, maintain world state, and run chaincode that endorses transactions. Because a peer stores mutable ledger data on disk under /var/hyperledger/production, it cannot be treated as an ephemeral pod. If a pod restarts or gets rescheduled, losing that directory means losing the ledger state. Kubernetes StatefulSets provide stable network identities and let you define volumeClaimTemplates so each replica gets its own persistent volume claim. This preserves ledger continuity across restarts. In practice, a peer StatefulSet specifies the hyperledger/fabric-peer image, mounts for MSP and TLS, and environment variables such as CORE_PEER_ID, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED, and CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE. A common misconception is to treat peers like stateless microservices; doing so causes data loss. A quick concrete example: if peer0 restarts and its PVC was not bound, the peer will start with an empty ledger and will fail to sync until you restore or reseed the ledger. Key verification steps include confirming each pod has a bound PVC and that the peer sees its MSP and TLS files mounted correctly. A final takeaway: treat peers as stateful first-class citizens and plan storage and identity mounts when you design manifests.

A peer StatefulSet is more than an image reference; it codifies the peer's runtime identity, storage, and security posture. The main components to include are the container image (hyperledger/fabric-peer), the environment variables that tell the peer its identity and TLS configuration, mounts for MSP and TLS secrets, and a volumeClaimTemplates block for ledger persistence. Environment variables like CORE_PEER_ID and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS establish how the peer identifies itself on the network. CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID sets the organization MSP ID, and CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED controls whether TLS is required. If you use CouchDB, CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE should be set to couchdb and the address provided via CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS. A common error is referencing service names that don't exist; double-check service DNS names and ports, and confirm that the CouchDB service is reachable from the peer namespace. As a practical check, ensure your CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH and TLS cert paths point to mounted secrets. When you roll out the StatefulSet, verify pod startup, PVC binding, and that the peer logs show a successful identity load. These pieces together make a robust peer manifest for production Kubernetes deployments. Persistent storage is essential to maintain peer ledger integrity. For the peer's /var/hyperledger/production directory, define a PersistentVolumeClaim through the StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates so each peer replica receives its own PVC. If your cluster supports dynamic provisioning, reference a StorageClass; otherwise pre-provision PVs matching the access mode and capacity. When using CouchDB as the state database, deploy CouchDB as its own StatefulSet and expose it with a headless Service so peers can reach particular CouchDB instances. The peer should reference that service through CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS. Always verify PV/PVC status and pod events if a peer pod remains pending. The key is to design storage with replication and retention suitable for your availability needs and confirm mounts at runtime. Administrative operations such as creating channels and joining peers are one-off tasks that fit the Kubernetes Job abstraction. A Job runs a pod to completion and ensures the specified number of successful runs. Define a Job that uses a fabric-tools image, mount the peer and orderer crypto via Secrets, and pass environment variables like CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, and ORDERER_TLS_ROOTCERT. A typical Job sequence fetches the channel configuration block, runs peer channel create with the orderer address and TLS cafile, then runs peer channel join and optional anchor peer updates. The chapter provides a clear example of a join-job YAML that mounts mychannel. block from a ConfigMap and executes peer channel join -b /etc/hyperledger/fabric/channel-artifacts/mychannel. block. Common mistakes include missing file mounts or incorrect CORE_PEER_ADDRESS that cause the peer CLI to fail. To debug, inspect the job pod logs with kubectl logs and check job status with kubectl get jobs. Jobs make administrative steps reproducible and auditable within Kubernetes, which is a major operational benefit for running Fabric in cluster environments. Let's walk through a concrete join Job example to make the process concrete. Deploying chaincode on a Kubernetes-managed Fabric network follows the standard Fabric lifecycle but each step can be executed inside Jobs so the cluster tracks work and artifacts. The lifecycle steps are: package the chaincode into a tar. gz with peer lifecycle chaincode package, install the package on each peer using peer lifecycle chaincode install, have each organization approve the chaincode definition using peer lifecycle chaincode approveformyorg, and finally commit the chaincode definition with peer lifecycle chaincode commit once enough approvals exist. In Kubernetes, create a sequence of Jobs for each step or a single Job that runs a script performing the ordered steps. Chaincode source can be baked into the fabric-tools image for development, or mounted from a ConfigMap or shared Persistent Volume in more advanced scenarios. Use explicit package IDs from the install output and forward them to approval commands. A misconception is assuming chaincode install auto-approves the definition; install is local to a peer, but approval is an org-level configuration step recorded on the channel. Always capture Job logs and check approval status with peer lifecycle chaincode queryapproved to confirm readiness before committing. Organizing lifecycle steps as Jobs makes chaincode operations reproducible and CI-friendly.

When you prepare chaincode for deployment in Kubernetes, you have three common strategies: bake chaincode into a custom fabric-tools image, mount the chaincode from a ConfigMap, or provide it via a shared Persistent Volume. Baking chaincode into an image simplifies development and ensures the package is available when the Job runs, but it requires image builds and pushes for each chaincode change. Using ConfigMaps works for small codebases and quick iteration, but ConfigMaps have size limitations and are less suitable for large binary artifacts. A shared Persistent Volume allows larger artifacts and is convenient in CI/CD pipelines where build artifacts are stored centrally, but it requires PV lifecycle management and access controls. The chapter warns that for production you may prefer CI/CD-managed images or PVs to avoid ephemeral ConfigMap limitations. A common misconception is that installing chaincode on a peer equals committing it to the channel — install is local, while approval and commit are channel operations that must be coordinated. Choose the packaging approach that fits your workflow: image for controlled release, PV for large teams and CI, and ConfigMap for small demos and quick tests.

Cryptographic materials must be provided to peers and to the fabric-tools containers that run admin commands. The recommended pattern is to generate MSP and TLS artifacts using fabric-ca-client or your chosen tooling, then place those artifacts into Kubernetes Secrets (for private keys and certs) and ConfigMaps (for non-sensitive artifacts like channel blocks). The peer StatefulSet mounts those Secrets at paths referenced by CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH and TLS variables so the peer loads its identity on startup. Jobs also mount the same secrets so fabric-tools can act as an org admin for channel creation and chaincode approval. A common mistake is encoding files incorrectly or placing private keys in non-secret ConfigMaps; always base64-encode and store sensitive files in Secrets. Another practical check is verifying file paths inside the running pod with kubectl exec to ensure the peer or job container sees the expected files and permissions. Remember that secrets mounted as files still respect Kubernetes RBAC and pod security policies, so align cluster-level security with your certificate handling practices. Proper secret management prevents startup failures and protects private keys in production environments. In production deployments, a few recurring problems tend to cause the most downtime. Incorrect service endpoints are common: if a peer's CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, ORDERER_ADDRESS, or CouchDB service names and ports are wrong, the peer or fabric CLI will fail to connect. Missing crypto material mounted incorrectly causes peers to fail at startup because MSP directories or TLS certs are not found. Persistent Volume issues—PVCs not binding to PVs—lead to peers starting with empty ledgers or failing to start entirely. Job failures often stem from incorrect peer CLI commands or missing environment variables and mounted files. Effective troubleshooting follows a pattern: check pod status and events with kubectl describe pod, inspect PVC and PV bindings with kubectl get pvc and kubectl describe pv, and view job pod logs with kubectl logs. For example, if a peer restarts and its ledger is empty, the most likely cause is an unbound PVC. If a job pod shows file-not-found errors, review volume mounts and ConfigMap/Secret names. These checks allow you to remediate quickly by fixing service names, recreating secrets, or provisioning PVs. Logging and consistent Jobs make it easier to reproduce and correct failures.

Next, base64-encode required files and create Kubernetes Secrets for the peer MSP and TLS, plus a ConfigMap for the channel block artifact. Here are the essential ideas to carry forward. First, peer deployment must treat peers as stateful: use StatefulSets and PVCs to ensure stable identity and durable ledger storage. Second, when using CouchDB, deploy it as its own StatefulSet and point the peer to its service endpoint so the peer uses the document store for world state. Third, the chaincode lifecycle remains packaging, installing, approving, and committing; each step can be run reliably inside Kubernetes Jobs so your operational steps are reproducible and auditable. Keep these three ideas in mind as you design manifests and run administrative operations in cluster environments.
